books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs
The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy

stimulus.text: In November 1832, a South Carolina convention declared the federal tariff acts of 1828 and 1832 null and void inside the state. President Andrew Jackson answered in a proclamation on December 10, 1832: 'The Constitution of the United States forms a government, not a league... I consider the power to annul a law of the United States incompatible with the existence of the Union, contradicted expressly by the letter of the Constitution, and destructive of the great object for which it was formed.' In a Senate debate in January 1830, Daniel Webster had closed with the words: 'Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!'
stimulus.source_note: Quotations: Andrew Jackson, Proclamation on Nullification, December 10, 1832, and Daniel Webster, Second Reply to Hayne, January 26, 1830. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The nullification crisis best illustrates which tension in Jackson's presidency?

options.text: Jackson consistently favored federal power over the states in every crisis
options.misconception: Jackson threatened South Carolina with troops, so it is easy to call him a federal-power president throughout.

options.text: Jackson consistently favored the states over the Union in every crisis
options.misconception: Jackson came from a states'-rights tradition, so it is easy to call him a states'-rights president throughout.

options.text: Jackson opposed all protective tariffs in every form
options.misconception: Jackson fought the 'Tariff of Abominations,' so it is easy to think he opposed all tariffs.

options.text: Jackson backed states' rights except when a state defied the Union

rationales.A: Jackson let Georgia defy the Supreme Court over the Cherokee, so he did not consistently favor federal power.
rationales.B: Jackson pushed the Force Bill through Congress and threatened troops, so he did not consistently favor the states.
rationales.C: Jackson signed the Tariff of 1832 into law; he opposed the Bank and high rates, not every tariff.
rationales.D: Jackson sided with Georgia against the Court on removal, yet threatened force against South Carolina: states' rights stopped where defiance of the Union began.
rationales.general:
1. Set the two cases side by side. On removal Jackson let a state defy the Court; on nullification he threatened a state with troops.
2. Find the line between them. Georgia's defiance served his policy, while South Carolina's defiance struck at the Union itself.
Background: Jackson came from a southern states'-rights tradition, but as president he defended the Union first.
Remember: when one leader acts both ways, look for the line that separates the two cases.
